```text
1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	We present a KL distillation framework for training contextual sparsity predictors in SwiGLU-based language models.
5	The method replaces per-neuron binary classification (BCE) with an output-distribution objective that couples all pruning decisions through the model's forward pass and achieves competitive performance without auxiliary error compensation networks at inference.
6	
7	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
8	\label{sec:method:formulation}
9	
10	Consider a pretrained transformer with $L$ layers, each containing a SwiGLU feed-forward network~\cite{shazeer2020glu}.
11	For layer $\ell$, the FFN computes:
12	\begin{align}
13	\mathbf{y}^{(\ell)} = \bigl(\sigma(\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)} \mathbf{W}_g^{(\ell)}) \odot \mathbf{x}^{(\ell)} \mathbf{W}_u^{(\ell)}\bigr) \mathbf{W}_d^{(\ell)},
14	\label{eq:swiglu}
15	\end{align}
16	where $\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the hidden state after attention ($d{=}4096$), $\sigma$ denotes SiLU, $\mathbf{W}_g^{(\ell)}, \mathbf{W}_u^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_{\text{ff}}}$ and $\mathbf{W}_d^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}} \times d}$ are the gate, up-projection, and down-projection matrices, and $d_{\text{ff}}{=}14{,}336$.
17	
18	Define the gate activation $\mathbf{g}^{(\ell)} = \sigma(\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)} \mathbf{W}_g^{(\ell)}) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}}$.
19	Each element $g_j^{(\ell)}$ determines the contribution of neuron $j$ to the output.
20	We introduce a binary mask $\mathbf{m}^{(\ell)} \in \{0,1\}^{d_{\text{ff}}}$ that zeros out pruned neurons:
21	\begin{align}
22	\mathbf{y}_{\text{sparse}}^{(\ell)} = \bigl(\mathbf{m}^{(\ell)} \odot \mathbf{g}^{(\ell)} \odot \mathbf{x}^{(\ell)} \mathbf{W}_u^{(\ell)}\bigr) \mathbf{W}_d^{(\ell)}.
23	\label{eq:sparse_ffn}
24	\end{align}
25	Our goal is to learn a mask predictor $f_\theta^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{h}) \to \mathbf{s}^{(\ell)} \in (0,1)^{d_{\text{ff}}}$ that produces per-neuron importance scores from the pre-FFN hidden state $\mathbf{h}$.
26	At inference, the scores are fed to a global top-$k$ allocation mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal} that distributes the sparsity budget across layers non-uniformly, retaining the $(1{-}\rho) \times L \times d_{\text{ff}}$ highest-scoring neurons model-wide for a target sparsity ratio $\rho$.
27	
28	
29	\subsection{Predictor Architecture}
30	\label{sec:method:predictor}
31	
32	Each layer $\ell$ has an independent two-layer MLP predictor:
33	\begin{align}
34	f_\theta^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{h}) = \text{GELU}(\mathbf{h} \mathbf{W}_1^{(\ell)}) \, \mathbf{W}_2^{(\ell)},
35	\label{eq:predictor}
36	\end{align}
37	where $\mathbf{W}_1^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_b}$ and $\mathbf{W}_2^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_b \times d_{\text{ff}}}$ with bottleneck dimension $d_b{=}128$.
38	The predictor takes the hidden state after attention (before the FFN) and outputs $d_{\text{ff}}$-dimensional logits $\mathbf{s}^{(\ell)}$, from which the mask is derived.
39	
40	Each predictor has $(4096 \times 128) + (128 \times 14336) = 2.37\text{M}$ parameters.
41	With 32 independent predictors (one per layer), the total overhead is 75.9M parameters, less than 1\% of the 8B base model.
42	The predictors operate independently across layers, requiring no cross-layer communication at inference.
43	
44	
45	\subsection{Gumbel-Sigmoid Relaxation}
46	\label{sec:method:gumbel}
47	
48	The hard mask $m_j = \mathbf{1}[s_j > \text{threshold}]$ is non-differentiable, preventing gradient flow from the KL objective through the mask to the predictor parameters.
49	We apply Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} to produce differentiable soft masks:
50	\begin{align}
51	\tilde{m}_j = \sigma_\tau\!\left(\log \frac{s_j}{1 - s_j} + g_1 - g_2\right), \quad g_1, g_2 \sim \text{Gumbel}(0,1),
52	\label{eq:gumbel}
53	\end{align}
54	where $\sigma_\tau(x) = \text{sigmoid}(x / \tau)$ and $\tau$ is a temperature parameter.
55	The Gumbel noise provides stochastic exploration of mask configurations during training, while the temperature controls sharpness: as $\tau \to 0$, $\tilde{m}_j$ approaches a binary decision.
56	
57	We anneal $\tau$ linearly from 1.0 to 0.1 over training.
58	At high temperature, the soft mask permits gradient flow through all neurons for broad exploration.
59	As temperature decreases, the mask concentrates on confident decisions, approximating the hard allocation used at inference.
60	
61	\paragraph{Comparison with Straight-Through Estimation.}
62	The straight-through estimator (STE)~\cite{bengio2013ste} applies a hard threshold in the forward pass and passes gradients through unchanged ($\partial m / \partial s = 1$).
63	In our setting, STE produces discontinuous gradient signals: small parameter changes can flip many neurons simultaneously, causing violent oscillations in the penalty weight and failure to converge to the target sparsity.
64	Gumbel relaxation eliminates this pathology, contributing a 34.5\% improvement (PPL 15.77 $\to$ 11.79 at 50\% sparsity), as we verify empirically in \S\ref{sec:experiments}.
65	
66	
67	\subsection{KL Divergence Training Objective}
68	\label{sec:method:kl}
69	
70	Let $\mathbf{z}_{\text{dense}}$ denote the output logits from a full dense forward pass, and $\mathbf{z}_{\text{sparse}}$ the logits from a forward pass with predictor-generated soft masks $\{\tilde{\mathbf{m}}^{(\ell)}\}_\ell$ applied at every layer.
71	We minimize the forward KL divergence between the dense and sparse output distributions:
72	\begin{align}
73	\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} = D_{\text{KL}}(p_{\text{dense}} \,\|\, p_{\text{sparse}}) = \sum_{v} p_{\text{dense}}^{(v)} \log \frac{p_{\text{dense}}^{(v)}}{p_{\text{sparse}}^{(v)}},
74	\label{eq:kl_loss}
75	\end{align}
76	where $p_{\text{dense}} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{\text{dense}})$ and $p_{\text{sparse}} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{\text{sparse}})$, summed over the vocabulary $v$ and averaged over sequence positions.
77	The base model is frozen; only the predictor parameters receive gradients.
78	
79	We use forward KL (mean-seeking) rather than reverse KL, as the goal is to preserve the dense model's primary predictions rather than explore alternative modes; \S\ref{sec:experiments} validates this choice with ablations over divergence direction (forward KL outperforms JSD by 6.4\% and reverse KL by 8.6\%).
80	No temperature scaling ($T{=}1$) is applied~\cite{hinton2015distilling}.
81	
82	
83	\subsection{Adaptive Penalty Sparsity Controller}
84	\label{sec:method:lagrangian}
85	
86	We enforce a model-level sparsity target $\rho$ via constrained optimization.
87	Let $\bar{s} = \frac{1}{L} \sum_\ell \frac{1}{d_{\text{ff}}} \sum_j \tilde{m}_j^{(\ell)}$ denote the average fraction of retained neurons.
88	The constrained problem is:
89	\begin{align}
90	\min_\theta \; \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \bar{s} \leq 1 - \rho.
91	\label{eq:constrained}
92	\end{align}
93	We relax this via an adaptive penalty controller:
94	\begin{align}
95	\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} + \lambda \cdot \text{clamp}(|\bar{s} - (1 - \rho)| - \epsilon, \min{=}0)^2,
96	\label{eq:lagrangian}
97	\end{align}
98	where $\epsilon = 0.02$ is a deadzone margin that prevents $\lambda$ from responding to small constraint violations.
99	The penalty weight $\lambda$ is updated multiplicatively at each step:
100	\begin{align}
101	\lambda \leftarrow \begin{cases} \lambda \times 2 & \text{if } \bar{s} > (1-\rho) + \epsilon \\ \lambda \times 0.5 & \text{if } \bar{s} < (1-\rho) - \epsilon \\ \lambda & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
102	\label{eq:dual_update}
103	\end{align}
104	with $\lambda$ clamped to $[\lambda_{\text{floor}}, \lambda_{\max}]$ where $\lambda_{\text{floor}} = 0.01$ and $\lambda_{\max} \in \{1000, 5000\}$ depending on the target.
105	The geometric doubling requires only $\lambda_{\max}$ as a user-specified hyperparameter (no step-size tuning) and reaches target sparsity within 40--110 steps for 40--50\% targets; for 30\% and 70\% targets, $\lambda$ saturates at $\lambda_{\max}$ with 1.7--5.0\% residual deviation (Appendix~\ref{app:lagrangian}, Figure~\ref{fig:lagrangian_dynamics}). The deadzone prevents oscillation once sparsity is within $\pm$2\%.\footnote{Our update rule resembles the augmented Lagrangian method but replaces gradient-based dual updates with a multiplicative schedule for training stability. We term it an adaptive penalty controller to distinguish from formal dual methods that guarantee KKT satisfaction.}
106	
107	
108	\subsection{Gradient Analysis: BCE vs.\ KL}
109	\label{sec:method:gradient}
110	
111	To build intuition for how KL distillation discovers neuron importance patterns that diverge from magnitude-based masks (\S\ref{sec:mask_analysis}), we contrast the gradient structure of the two objectives. This analysis is suggestive; \S\ref{sec:mask_analysis} provides causal confirmation that mask target quality, not gradient coupling, drives KL's advantage.
112	
113	Under BCE, the predictor trains against oracle masks $m_j^* = \mathbf{1}[|g_j| \geq \text{top-}k\text{ threshold}]$ derived from activation magnitudes.
114	The gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$; each neuron is trained independently with no inter-neuron coupling.
115	Under KL distillation, the chain rule introduces a downstream Jacobian $\partial \mathbf{z}_{\text{sparse}} / \partial \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}$ that couples neuron $j$'s gradient to all other retained neurons in layers $\ell$ through $L$, because the sparse hidden state propagates through subsequent attention and FFN operations.
116	This coupling allows KL to evaluate each neuron's importance in context of the full sparse computation, rather than against a fixed magnitude target.
117	
118	Gradient SNR measurements\footnote{$\text{SNR}_\ell = \|\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\theta_\ell} \mathcal{L}]\|_2^2 / \text{Var}[\nabla_{\theta_\ell} \mathcal{L}]$, expectation over mini-batches.} confirm a structural difference: at convergence, KL achieves $5.14\times$ higher SNR than BCE ($5.877{\times}10^{-3}$ vs.\ $1.144{\times}10^{-3}$, LLaMA-3.1-8B, C4; Appendix~\ref{app:snr_extended}).
119	The coupled gradient provides a mechanism by which KL can discover mask patterns that diverge from magnitude ranking; the causal ablation in \S\ref{sec:mask_analysis} confirms that these patterns, not the coupling itself, are responsible for the quality advantage.
120	
121	\subsection{Two-Dimensional Taxonomy of Sparsity Prediction Methods}
122	\label{sec:method:taxonomy}
123	
124	We organize prior work along two axes: \emph{correction granularity} (how the mask adapts to input) and \emph{training signal coupling} (whether the objective captures inter-neuron dependencies).
125	
126	\begin{table}[t]
127	\centering
128	\caption{Taxonomy of learned sparsity prediction methods along correction granularity (rows) and training signal coupling (columns). Our method fills the previously unexplored Per-token $\times$ Coupled cell.}
129	\label{tab:taxonomy}
130	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
131	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
132	\toprule
133	 & Decomposed (BCE) & Intermediate (MSE) & Coupled (KL) \\
134	\midrule
135	Static & --- & --- & SPON \\
136	Per-token & DejaVu, FastForward & ShadowLLM, D2DMoE & \textbf{Ours} \\
137	\bottomrule
138	\end{tabular}}
139	\end{table}
140	
141	\paragraph{Correction granularity.}
142	\emph{Static} methods~\cite{xu2026spon} learn a fixed bias vector per layer that does not depend on the input token.
143	\emph{Per-token} methods~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward,akhauri2024shadowllm,szatkowski2024d2dmoe} produce a unique mask for each input position, conditioning on the token's hidden state at each layer.
144	
145	\paragraph{Training signal coupling.}
146	\emph{Decomposed} objectives (BCE) treat each neuron independently, optimizing per-element classification against an oracle mask.
147	\emph{Intermediate} objectives (MSE on hidden states) capture local coupling within a single layer but not end-to-end output effects.
148	\emph{Coupled} objectives (KL on output distribution) propagate gradients through the full forward pass, reflecting how all mask decisions jointly affect the final distribution.
149	
150	SPON~\cite{xu2026spon} distills a per-layer bias via KL but cannot adapt to per-input neuron importance (static $\times$ coupled).
151	DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} and FastForward~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} achieve per-token granularity but use BCE, where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.
152	D2DMoE~\cite{szatkowski2024d2dmoe} provides intermediate coupling (MSE on hidden states) but not end-to-end output effects.
153	Our method combines per-token prediction with coupled KL training (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}), propagating gradients through all downstream layers.
154
```

```json
      "content": "\\section{Method}\n\\label{sec:method}\n\nWe present a KL distillation framework for training contextual sparsity predictors in SwiGLU-based language models.\nThe method replaces per-neuron binary classification (BCE) with an output-distribution objective that couples all pruning decisions through the model's forward pass and achieves competitive performance without auxiliary error compensation networks at inference.\n\n\\subsection{Problem Formulation}\n\\label{sec:method:formulation}\n\nConsider a pretrained transformer with $L$ layers, each containing a SwiGLU feed-forward network~\\cite{shazeer2020glu}.\nFor layer $\\ell$, the FFN computes:\n\\begin{align}\n\\mathbf{y}^{(\\ell)} = \\bigl(\\sigma(\\mathbf{x}^{(\\ell)} \\mathbf{W}_g^{(\\ell)}) \\odot \\mathbf{x}^{(\\ell)} \\mathbf{W}_u^{(\\ell)}\\bigr) \\mathbf{W}_d^{(\\ell)},\n\\label{eq:swiglu}\n\\end{align}\nwhere $\\mathbf{x}^{(\\ell)} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the hidden state after attention ($d{=}4096$), $\\sigma$ denotes SiLU, $\\mathbf{W}_g^{(\\ell)}, \\mathbf{W}_u^{(\\ell)} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d \\times d_{\\text{ff}}}$ and $\\mathbf{W}_d^{(\\ell)} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_{\\text{ff}} \\times d}$ are the gate, up-projection, and down-projection matrices, and $d_{\\text{ff}}{=}14{,}336$.\n\nDefine the gate activation $\\mathbf{g}^{(\\ell)} = \\sigma(\\mathbf{x}^{(\\ell)} \\mathbf{W}_g^{(\\ell)}) \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_{\\text{ff}}}$.\nEach element $g_j^{(\\ell)}$ determines the contribution of neuron $j$ to the output.\nWe introduce a binary mask $\\mathbf{m}^{(\\ell)} \\in \\{0,1\\}^{d_{\\text{ff}}}$ that zeros out pruned neurons:\n\\begin{align}\n\\mathbf{y}_{\\text{sparse}}^{(\\ell)} = \\bigl(\\mathbf{m}^{(\\ell)} \\odot \\mathbf{g}^{(\\ell)} \\odot \\mathbf{x}^{(\\ell)} \\mathbf{W}_u^{(\\ell)}\\bigr) \\mathbf{W}_d^{(\\ell)}.\n\\label{eq:sparse_ffn}\n\\end{align}\nOur goal is to learn a mask predictor $f_\\theta^{(\\ell)}(\\mathbf{h}) \\to \\mathbf{s}^{(\\ell)} \\in (0,1)^{d_{\\text{ff}}}$ that produces per-neuron importance scores from the pre-FFN hidden state $\\mathbf{h}$.\nAt inference, the scores are fed to a global top-$k$ allocation mechanism~\\cite{liu2025teal} that distributes the sparsity budget across layers non-uniformly, retaining the $(1{-}\\rho) \\times L \\times d_{\\text{ff}}$ highest-scoring neurons model-wide for a target sparsity ratio $\\rho$.\n\n\n\\subsection{Predictor Architecture}\n\\label{sec:method:predictor}\n\nEach layer $\\ell$ has an independent two-layer MLP predictor:\n\\begin{align}\nf_\\theta^{(\\ell)}(\\mathbf{h}) = \\text{GELU}(\\mathbf{h} \\mathbf{W}_1^{(\\ell)}) \\, \\mathbf{W}_2^{(\\ell)},\n\\label{eq:predictor}\n\\end{align}\nwhere $\\mathbf{W}_1^{(\\ell)} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d \\times d_b}$ and $\\mathbf{W}_2^{(\\ell)} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d_b \\times d_{\\text{ff}}}$ with bottleneck dimension $d_b{=}128$.\nThe predictor takes the hidden state after attention (before the FFN) and outputs $d_{\\text{ff}}$-dimensional logits $\\mathbf{s}^{(\\ell)}$, from which the mask is derived.\n\nEach predictor has $(4096 \\times 128) + (128 \\times 14336) = 2.37\\text{M}$ parameters.\nWith 32 independent predictors (one per layer), the total overhead is 75.9M parameters, less than 1\\% of the 8B base model.\nThe predictors operate independently across layers, requiring no cross-layer communication at inference.\n\n\n\\subsection{Gumbel-Sigmoid Relaxation}\n\\label{sec:method:gumbel}\n\nThe hard mask $m_j = \\mathbf{1}[s_j > \\text{threshold}]$ is non-differentiable, preventing gradient flow from the KL objective through the mask to the predictor parameters.\nWe apply Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\\cite{jang2017gumbel} to produce differentiable soft masks:\n\\begin{align}\n\\tilde{m}_j = \\sigma_\\tau\\!\\left(\\log \\frac{s_j}{1 - s_j} + g_1 - g_2\\right), \\quad g_1, g_2 \\sim \\text{Gumbel}(0,1),\n\\label{eq:gumbel}\n\\end{align}\nwhere $\\sigma_\\tau(x) = \\text{sigmoid}(x / \\tau)$ and $\\tau$ is a temperature parameter.\nThe Gumbel noise provides stochastic exploration of mask configurations during training, while the temperature controls sharpness: as $\\tau \\to 0$, $\\tilde{m}_j$ approaches a binary decision.\n\nWe anneal $\\tau$ linearly from 1.0 to 0.1 over training.\nAt high temperature, the soft mask permits gradient flow through all neurons for broad exploration.\nAs temperature decreases, the mask concentrates on confident decisions, approximating the hard allocation used at inference.\n\n\\paragraph{Comparison with Straight-Through Estimation.}\nThe straight-through estimator (STE)~\\cite{bengio2013ste} applies a hard threshold in the forward pass and passes gradients through unchanged ($\\partial m / \\partial s = 1$).\nIn our setting, STE produces discontinuous gradient signals: small parameter changes can flip many neurons simultaneously, causing violent oscillations in the penalty weight and failure to converge to the target sparsity.\nGumbel relaxation eliminates this pathology, contributing a 34.5\\% improvement (PPL 15.77 $\\to$ 11.79 at 50\\% sparsity), as we verify empirically in \\S\\ref{sec:experiments}.\n\n\n\\subsection{KL Divergence Training Objective}\n\\label{sec:method:kl}\n\nLet $\\mathbf{z}_{\\text{dense}}$ denote the output logits from a full dense forward pass, and $\\mathbf{z}_{\\text{sparse}}$ the logits from a forward pass with predictor-generated soft masks $\\{\\tilde{\\mathbf{m}}^{(\\ell)}\\}_\\ell$ applied at every layer.\nWe minimize the forward KL divergence between the dense and sparse output distributions:\n\\begin{align}\n\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{KL}} = D_{\\text{KL}}(p_{\\text{dense}} \\,\\|\\, p_{\\text{sparse}}) = \\sum_{v} p_{\\text{dense}}^{(v)} \\log \\frac{p_{\\text{dense}}^{(v)}}{p_{\\text{sparse}}^{(v)}},\n\\label{eq:kl_loss}\n\\end{align}\nwhere $p_{\\text{dense}} = \\text{softmax}(\\mathbf{z}_{\\text{dense}})$ and $p_{\\text{sparse}} = \\text{softmax}(\\mathbf{z}_{\\text{sparse}})$, summed over the vocabulary $v$ and averaged over sequence positions.\nThe base model is frozen; only the predictor parameters receive gradients.\n\nWe use forward KL (mean-seeking) rather than reverse KL, as the goal is to preserve the dense model's primary predictions rather than explore alternative modes; \\S\\ref{sec:experiments} validates this choice with ablations over divergence direction (forward KL outperforms JSD by 6.4\\% and reverse KL by 8.6\\%).\nNo temperature scaling ($T{=}1$) is applied~\\cite{hinton2015distilling}.\n\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Penalty Sparsity Controller}\n\\label{sec:method:lagrangian}\n\nWe enforce a model-level sparsity target $\\rho$ via constrained optimization.\nLet $\\bar{s} = \\frac{1}{L} \\sum_\\ell \\frac{1}{d_{\\text{ff}}} \\sum_j \\tilde{m}_j^{(\\ell)}$ denote the average fraction of retained neurons.\nThe constrained problem is:\n\\begin{align}\n\\min_\\theta \\; \\mathcal{L}_{\\text{KL}} \\quad \\text{s.t.} \\quad \\bar{s} \\leq 1 - \\rho.\n\\label{eq:constrained}\n\\end{align}\nWe relax this via an adaptive penalty controller:\n\\begin{align}\n\\mathcal{L} = \\mathcal{L}_{\\text{KL}} + \\lambda \\cdot \\text{clamp}(|\\bar{s} - (1 - \\rho)| - \\epsilon, \\min{=}0)^2,\n\\label{eq:lagrangian}\n\\end{align}\nwhere $\\epsilon = 0.02$ is a deadzone margin that prevents $\\lambda$ from responding to small constraint violations.\nThe penalty weight $\\lambda$ is updated multiplicatively at each step:\n\\begin{align}\n\\lambda \\leftarrow \\begin{cases} \\lambda \\times 2 & \\text{if } \\bar{s} > (1-\\rho) + \\epsilon \\\\ \\lambda \\times 0.5 & \\text{if } \\bar{s} < (1-\\rho) - \\epsilon \\\\ \\lambda & \\text{otherwise} \\end{cases}\n\\label{eq:dual_update}\n\\end{align}\nwith $\\lambda$ clamped to $[\\lambda_{\\text{floor}}, \\lambda_{\\max}]$ where $\\lambda_{\\text{floor}} = 0.01$ and $\\lambda_{\\max} \\in \\{1000, 5000\\}$ depending on the target.\nThe geometric doubling requires only $\\lambda_{\\max}$ as a user-specified hyperparameter (no step-size tuning) and reaches target sparsity within 40--110 steps for 40--50\\% targets; for 30\\% and 70\\% targets, $\\lambda$ saturates at $\\lambda_{\\max}$ with 1.7--5.0\\% residual deviation (Appendix~\\ref{app:lagrangian}, Figure~\\ref{fig:lagrangian_dynamics}). The deadzone prevents oscillation once sparsity is within $\\pm$2\\%.\\footnote{Our update rule resembles the augmented Lagrangian method but replaces gradient-based dual updates with a multiplicative schedule for training stability. We term it an adaptive penalty controller to distinguish from formal dual methods that guarantee KKT satisfaction.}\n\n\n\\subsection{Gradient Analysis: BCE vs.\\ KL}\n\\label{sec:method:gradient}\n\nTo build intuition for how KL distillation discovers neuron importance patterns that diverge from magnitude-based masks (\\S\\ref{sec:mask_analysis}), we contrast the gradient structure of the two objectives. This analysis is suggestive; \\S\\ref{sec:mask_analysis} provides causal confirmation that mask target quality, not gradient coupling, drives KL's advantage.\n\nUnder BCE, the predictor trains against oracle masks $m_j^* = \\mathbf{1}[|g_j| \\geq \\text{top-}k\\text{ threshold}]$ derived from activation magnitudes.\nThe gradient $\\partial \\mathcal{L}_{\\text{BCE}} / \\partial s_j = \\sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$; each neuron is trained independently with no inter-neuron coupling.\nUnder KL distillation, the chain rule introduces a downstream Jacobian $\\partial \\mathbf{z}_{\\text{sparse}} / \\partial \\mathbf{h}^{(\\ell)}$ that couples neuron $j$'s gradient to all other retained neurons in layers $\\ell$ through $L$, because the sparse hidden state propagates through subsequent attention and FFN operations.\nThis coupling allows KL to evaluate each neuron's importance in context of the full sparse computation, rather than against a fixed magnitude target.\n\nGradient SNR measurements\\footnote{$\\text{SNR}_\\ell = \\|\\mathbb{E}[\\nabla_{\\theta_\\ell} \\mathcal{L}]\\|_2^2 / \\text{Var}[\\nabla_{\\theta_\\ell} \\mathcal{L}]$, expectation over mini-batches.} confirm a structural difference: at convergence, KL achieves $5.14\\times$ higher SNR than BCE ($5.877{\\times}10^{-3}$ vs.\\ $1.144{\\times}10^{-3}$, LLaMA-3.1-8B, C4; Appendix~\\ref{app:snr_extended}).\nThe coupled gradient provides a mechanism by which KL can discover mask patterns that diverge from magnitude ranking; the causal ablation in \\S\\ref{sec:mask_analysis} confirms that these patterns, not the coupling itself, are responsible for the quality advantage.\n\n\\subsection{Two-Dimensional Taxonomy of Sparsity Prediction Methods}\n\\label{sec:method:taxonomy}\n\nWe organize prior work along two axes: \\emph{correction granularity} (how the mask adapts to input) and \\emph{training signal coupling} (whether the objective captures inter-neuron dependencies).\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Taxonomy of learned sparsity prediction methods along correction granularity (rows) and training signal coupling (columns). Our method fills the previously unexplored Per-token $\\times$ Coupled cell.}\n\\label{tab:taxonomy}\n\\resizebox{\\columnwidth}{!}{\n\\begin{tabular}{lccc}\n\\toprule\n & Decomposed (BCE) & Intermediate (MSE) & Coupled (KL) \\\\\n\\midrule\nStatic & --- & --- & SPON \\\\\nPer-token & DejaVu, FastForward & ShadowLLM, D2DMoE & \\textbf{Ours} \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\paragraph{Correction granularity.}\n\\emph{Static} methods~\\cite{xu2026spon} learn a fixed bias vector per layer that does not depend on the input token.\n\\emph{Per-token} methods~\\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward,akhauri2024shadowllm,szatkowski2024d2dmoe} produce a unique mask for each input position, conditioning on the token's hidden state at each layer.\n\n\\paragraph{Training signal coupling.}\n\\emph{Decomposed} objectives (BCE) treat each neuron independently, optimizing per-element classification against an oracle mask.\n\\emph{Intermediate} objectives (MSE on hidden states) capture local coupling within a single layer but not end-to-end output effects.\n\\emph{Coupled} objectives (KL on output distribution) propagate gradients through the full forward pass, reflecting how all mask decisions jointly affect the final distribution.\n\nSPON~\\cite{xu2026spon} distills a per-layer bias via KL but cannot adapt to per-input neuron importance (static $\\times$ coupled).\nDejaVu~\\cite{liu2023dejavu} and FastForward~\\cite{gautam2026fastforward} achieve per-token granularity but use BCE, where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.\nD2DMoE~\\cite{szatkowski2024d2dmoe} provides intermediate coupling (MSE on hidden states) but not end-to-end output effects.\nOur method combines 1	\section*{Ethics Statement}
```
```text
2	
3	This work proposes a training method for sparsity predictors in pretrained language models, evaluated on publicly available models (LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3) and standard benchmarks (WikiText-2, WikiText-103, C4, ARC, WinoGrande, MMLU, GSM8K).
4	No new data collection, annotation, or human subjects are involved.
5	The method does not alter model outputs beyond the sparsity-induced degradation we analyze; it introduces no new generation capabilities or safety risks beyond those inherent in the base models.
6	Compute requirements are modest (1000 training steps, $\sim$45 minutes on a single GPU for KL training), presenting minimal environmental concern relative to the pretrained models we evaluate on.
7	We release no model weights or user-facing systems; our contribution is analytical (understanding KL distillation for sparsity) rather than deployment-oriented.
```

<details><summary>↩ Tool result · `toolu_01XW7zpsKgRX1xZhEwuCHNrm`</summary>

```text
1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	SwiGLU feed-forward networks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} in modern LLMs exhibit high contextual sparsity: at any given token, a large fraction of FFN neurons contribute negligibly to the output.
4	Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they universally rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
5	Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: TEAL's top-$k$ mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal} ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
6	This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.
7	
8	Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
9	This suggests KL should outperform BCE under global allocation.
10	The empirical picture, however, reveals something more fundamental: KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 32\%), and a causal ablation confirms that these learned mask patterns, not gradient coupling, are the primary quality driver.
11	Under controlled 50\% evaluation, BCE trained on KL-derived targets exactly matches KL across perplexity and all downstream tasks (max $\Delta$=0.59pp, 2-seed), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\pm$0.20.
12	
13	We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
14	With uniform allocation, the predictor achieves PPL 11.92 at 50\% sparsity (3-seed); under global top-$k$, PPL improves to 11.79 (49\% over TEAL).
15	At 30\% sparsity, global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed downstream standard deviation ($7.5\times$), making uniform allocation preferable for stability.
16	Evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} and Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} confirms the PPL advantage at 7--14B, though 14B exhibits an MMLU gap (63.7\% vs.\ TEAL's 71.8\%) not resolved by allocation strategy.
17	Our contribution is empirical: we characterize how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality, and analyze interactions between allocation strategy, sparsity level, and model scale. Wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).
18	
19	Our contributions are:
20	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
21	\item KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns diverging 68\% from magnitude-based masks. A causal ablation proves that mask target quality, not gradient coupling, determines quality under global allocation (\S\ref{sec:mask_analysis}).
22	\item These superior mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
23	\item Analysis of allocation-to-downstream interactions at 7--14B: non-monotonic allocation preference at 8B and scale-dependent effects at 14B (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
24	\end{itemize}
25
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Introduction}\n\nSwiGLU feed-forward networks~\\cite{shazeer2020glu} in modern LLMs exhibit high contextual sparsity: at any given token, a large fraction of FFN neurons contribute negligibly to the output.\nLearned sparsity predictors~\\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they universally rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.\nYet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: TEAL's top-$k$ mechanism~\\cite{liu2025teal} ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.\nThis mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.\n\nGradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\\partial \\mathcal{L}_{\\text{BCE}} / \\partial s_j = \\sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\\S\\ref{sec:method:gradient}).\nThis suggests KL should outperform BCE under global allocation.\nThe empirical picture, however, reveals something more fundamental: KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 32\\%), and a causal ablation confirms that these learned mask patterns, not gradient coupling, are the primary quality driver.\nUnder controlled 50\\% evaluation, BCE trained on KL-derived targets exactly matches KL across perplexity and all downstream tasks (max $\\Delta$=0.59pp, 2-seed), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\\pm$0.20.\n\nWe instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.\nWith uniform allocation, the predictor achieves PPL 11.92 at 50\\% sparsity (3-seed); under global top-$k$, PPL improves to 11.79 (49\\% over TEAL).\nAt 30\\% sparsity, global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed downstream standard deviation ($7.5\\times$), making uniform allocation preferable for stability.\nEvaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\\cite{jiang2023mistral} and Qwen-2.5-14B~\\cite{qwen2024qwen25} confirms the PPL advantage at 7--14B, though 14B exhibits an MMLU gap (63.7\\% vs.\\ TEAL's 71.8\\%) not resolved by allocation strategy.\nOur contribution is empirical: we characterize how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality, and analyze interactions between allocation strategy, sparsity level, and model scale. Wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here (Appendix~\\ref{app:latency}).\n\nOur contributions are:\n\\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]\n\\item KL-trained predictors discover neuron importance patterns diverging 68\\% from magnitude-based masks. A causal ablation proves that mask target quality, not gradient coupling, determines quality under global allocation (\\S\\ref{sec:mask_analysis}).\n\\item These superior mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\\S\\ref{sec:isocompute}).\n\\item Analysis of allocation-to-downstream interactions at 7--14B: non-monotonic allocation preference at 8B and scale-dependent effects at 14B (\\S\\ref{sec:scaling}).\n\\end{itemize}\n",
```
